newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian cooperation urged in fight against piracy, drugs.
newsitem.headline: Asian cooperation urged in fight against piracy, drugs.

text.p: Asia-Pacific countries must cooperate more in the battle against growing piracy, illegal migration and drug smuggling on the high seas, a maritime conference in Singapore was told.

Stanley Weeks, a senior security analyst with the U.S. Science Applications International Corp., said in a paper made available on Wednesday that piracy, drug smuggling and illegal migration were "serious enough to affect maritime security".
"There would be value in regional cooperation to address them, perhaps within the broader scope of regional or sub-regional maritime cooperation or safety agreements," he said.

The number of piracy incidents attacks on the world's seas rose sharply in 1995 to 170 from 92 the previous year, Weeks quoted the annual piracy report of the International Maritime Bureau (IMB) as saying.
Most incidents took place in the Asia-Pacific, where the number of reported piracy caes rose to 103 from 73 in 1994.
The IMB reported last month that global piracy attacks rose to 224 in 1996.

Weeks said the most dangerous waters for ships in the region remained those of the Indonesian archipelago and the triangle between China's Hainan Island, Hong Kong and the northern part of the Philippine island of Luzon.
More than 74 attacks took place in those two areas in 1995, more than in any other part of the region.
"It is...clear that discussions and cooperation between regional Asia-Pacific nations can help ensure effective crackdowns on piracy," Weeks said.

Hasjim Djalal, ambassador-at-large for maritime affairs in the Indonesia Foreign Ministry, said the problems there stem from the fact that Indonesia "now has maritime zones three times as large as its land territory".
"Indonesia needs a more maritime-oriented policy in facing the 21st century. Consequently, more attention and budget would have to be devoted to maritime and ocean affairs and development," he said.

Weeks said increased cooperation in battling piracy could also be extended to enhanced coordination in countering maritime drug trafficking and the illegal smuggling of people from places like China to as far as Canada and the United States.
"As with piracy and drug trafficking, procedures to detect and counter illegal migration by sea should be part of eventual regional (agreements)," he concluded.
